title: In CT models of 78 orbits, ultrasound through the closed eyelid and orbital roof resolves orbitofrontal blood-volume changes only in about 3-4 mm voxels under eye limits, coarser than 3T fMRI
abstract: Functional ultrasound can reach the orbitofrontal cortex through the closed eyelid and the thin bone above the eye (the orbital roof), but in a model built from 39 head CT scans it detects a typical blood-volume response there only in voxels of about 3-4 mm side in one minute: coarser than 3 tesla functional MRI (fMRI) and much coarser than 7 tesla fMRI. This matters because the orbitofrontal cortex is hard to measure (skull bone blocks ultrasound and light, and sinus air removes much of the fMRI signal there), and because it shows that the eye socket is a usable but marginal window to cortex, not a high-resolution one. We used 39 normal public head CTs (CQ500; 78 orbits), traced 111 million straight rays from the skin over each orbit to brain targets, and kept rays that cross no air, at most one bone layer and no possible lens position. Bone transmission came from an elastic plate model with shear waves, and sensitivity from a published power-Doppler noise model under the US eye limits (50 mW/cm2, mechanical index 0.23, and thermal index max(soft tissue, cranial bone) <= 1). The orbital roof is 1.52 mm thick per orbit (median; 10-90 percent of orbits 0.96-2.24 mm), close to caliper data. Usable rays meet it at about 38 degrees after 49 mm of tissue, half through the vitreous. The cranial-bone thermal index limits the face intensity to about 12 mW/cm2 over the 13 cm2 driven aperture, and the best frequency is about 1.5-1.8 MHz. For cortex within 10 mm above the roof (13 cm3 per orbit), base inputs give a median-orbit voxel of 2.9 mm (orbits 2.0-4.8 mm); 32 percent of targets beat a 3T fMRI model (2.28 mm) and 7.5 percent beat 7T (1.24 mm). Over 200 Monte Carlo draws the median-orbit voxel is 3.7 mm (90 percent interval 1.8-7.6 mm); where both methods detect, it beats paired 3T fMRI in 19 percent of draws, 3T fMRI with orbitofrontal signal loss in 21 percent, and 7T in none. One 30 mm probe with one frequency gives 3.3 mm, and the small window sets a floor near 2.1 mm. Roof thickness predicts the voxel per orbit (Spearman 0.86), and shear-wave and longitudinal loss in the roof decide most of the uncertainty. Main limits: straight rays, no choroid or vessel clutter, no eye motion, CT-based thickness. An independent review corrected the eye-safety limit and the orbit mask of the first version. A cadaver measurement of roof transmission at 1-3 MHz and 30-50 degrees would settle the decisive inputs.
